diagnosis: Ileocolic intussusception with a polypoid lead point
symptom: a tummy ache that comes and goes and jeans that feel looser lately
hook: A coiled spring stuffed inside a garden hose.
whatYouSee: A coiled-spring filling defect blocking the colon near the hepatic flexure on the right side of the patient.
whyItMatters: Intussusception shows as a coiled spring on contrast enema and a target sign on CT. In an adult with pain and anaemia and weight loss a polypoid mass is often the lead point.
treatment: If an adult has a mass at the lead point the involved bowel is usually resected surgically with histology. A contrast enema can be therapeutic mainly in children.
takeaway: A coiled spring on barium enema means bowel telescoping into bowel.

defects: Unexplained additional image findings: ["The coiled metallic object in the right upper quadrant appears as a tightly wound wire/spring device rather than the expected coiled-spring sign of barium trickling around an intussusceptum — its appearance is inconsistent with any explained anatomical structure or medical device in this clinical context"]

findings: Anteroposterior projection of the abdomen and pelvis
Barium contrast study of the large bowel (double-contrast barium enema technique): barium coats the mucosal surface of the entire colon with haustral pattern visible throughout
The colon is opacified from rectum through sigmoid, descending, transverse, and ascending colon to the cecum; the hepatic and splenic flexures are identified
A coiled metallic foreign body is present in the right upper quadrant overlying the region of the hepatic flexure/ascending colon — appears to be a tightly coiled wire or spring-like device
The colonic haustral folds appear preserved and symmetric throughout the visualised segments with no definite mucosal filling defect or apple-core lesion identified on this view
No free intraperitoneal gas is identified
Bony pelvis and visualised lumbar spine appear intact without overt lytic or sclerotic lesion
Soft tissue density in the pelvis likely represents urinary bladder filled with contrast or urine
differential: Double-contrast barium enema examination — the primary purpose of the study; the overall appearance is consistent with a technically adequate examination; no gross colonic pathology definitively identified on this single view

Retained or ingested metallic foreign body (coiled wire/spring) in the right upper quadrant — could represent an ingested object, a colonoscopy-related device (guidewire loop), or an extrinsic device; location adjacent to hepatic flexure raises concern for proximity to bowel wall

Colonic polyp or early mucosal lesion not excluded — single-view assessment is limited; additional projections (lateral, oblique, post-evacuation) would be required to evaluate for subtle filling defects
anatomyConcerns: The tightly coiled metallic object in the right upper quadrant is a significant acquisition/clinical inconsistency — its nature (intraluminal, intramural, or extrinsic) cannot be determined from this single projection alone
The rectosigmoid region appears incompletely distended relative to the rest of the colon, which may represent underfilling or true luminal narrowing; additional views needed
Only a single AP projection is available; standard double-contrast barium enema requires multiple projections (prone, oblique, lateral decubitus, post-evacuation) for complete mucosal assessment
